newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British government borrowing rises in May.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British government borrowing rises in May.

text.p: Britain reported a budget deficit of 3.96 billion pounds in May, nearly 1.0 billion above expectations, the Office for National Statistics said on Tuesday.
But analysts say the high borrowing figure is attributable to several special factors and there is still little justification for hefty tax rises in the new British government's budget on July 2.
"The figures are slightly disappointing. But we have had an extraordinarily good run in recent months, so this may be just one bad apple," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.
"The general trend is very strong -- good receipt growth coupled with reasonable restraint on the spending side," he said.

The higher than expected borrowing requirement for May follows an unexpectedly small deficit in April -- just 76 million pounds -- and the overall trend suggests the gap between government receipts and spending is continuing to narrow.
Revenue in April was boosted by tax on bonuses paid to financial sector workers as well as changes in the timing of payments of the British sales tax -- value added tax (VAT).
VAT payments in April were up 40 percent compared with a year earlier, while those for May 1997 were correspondingly depressed, down 11.5 percent on the same basis.
Analysts still expect Britain will undershoot the official forecast of a 19.2 billion pounds deficit by up to 5.0 billion this year.
The budget deficit for the first two months of the 1997-98 fiscal year shows a shortfall of 4.03 billion pounds, down 35 percent from the same period last year.

But given that the economy has been growing for five years, the figures are not good enough to stop Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown from raising taxes at all in his first budget, analysts said.

"The Chancellor is still likely to tighten fiscal policy modestly in the July budget in order to improve the medium- term outlook and provide room for some slippage on the spending plans," said Ciaran Barr, senior UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The May data provided some good news on government spending in the first two months of the financial year -- the figure is 2.0 percent lower than the same period last year.

But the ruling Labour Party, which ended the Conservatives' 18-year reign on May 1, is still likely to struggle to fulfil its pledge to stick to the previous administration's rigorous target of spending growth of just 2.0 percent over the next two years, analysts said.
This would mean higher taxes but the government will also be keen to avoid being seen to renege on election promises.

"Brown will certainly be very wary about breaking the spirit of his election, no tax-increase pledges. But he will want to tighten policy a little bit, perhaps three billion sterling of tightening," CIBC chief economist David Coleman said.
The budget is expected to raise revenue through changing the taxation of share dividends, in the form of advance corporation tax, which would mainly hit tax-exempt institutions such as pension funds.

Proceeds from the second round of payments on shares in the privatised British train network, Railtrack, swelled the government's coffers by 221 million pounds in May and the ONS said another 700 million instalment was likely in June.
